title: Checkpoint: Kinds of Government
objective: After this level you can compare the main kinds of government.
summary: Aristotle sorted governments by who rules and for whose benefit. Chapter 2's systems fit his grid, and modern questions add limits, federalism and whether the state works at all.

cards.headline: Aristotle sorted every government with two questions. They still work.
cards.body: Who rules: one person, a few, or the many? And for whose benefit: everyone's, or only the rulers' own? Cross the two questions and you get six kinds of government.

items.label: Rule by one
points: For the ruler's own good: tyranny

items.label: Rule by a few
points: For their own good: oligarchy, usually the wealthy

items.label: Rule by the many
points: For their own good: "democracy", in his sense rule by the poor

cards.headline: This chapter on his grid
cards.body: Place the chapter on Aristotle's grid. Louis XIV and Malaysia's paramount ruler are rule by one. Venice's Great Council is rule by a few. Glarus's raised hands are rule by the many. Aristotle's twist is that numbers aren't everything: a government is just, he argued, when it aims at the common advantage. Modern systems add questions he didn't ask. Is power limited, as in a constitutional monarchy? Is it split across the map, as in a federation? Does the state work at all?

mascot.line: Ten levels, a whole shelf of governments. You can now sort a history book's rulers by type.

cards.headline: Chapter 2 complete
learned: Aristotle: who rules, and for whose benefit?
Rule by one: monarchy, absolute or constitutional, and dictatorship
Rule by a few or by religion: oligarchy and theocracy
Rule by many: direct democracy and republics
Federal or unitary, and what happens when states fail

questions.prompt: Aristotle sorted governments by who rules. What was his second question?

options.label: How old the government is
options.rationale: Age wasn't one of his two questions.

options.label: Whose benefit the rulers rule for
Whether the ruler is religious
options.rationale: Religion wasn't one of his two questions.

options.label: How large the territory is
options.rationale: Size was Madison's concern, not Aristotle's sorting question.

questions.explanation: Aristotle asked who rules (one, few or many) and for whose benefit: the common good or the rulers' own.

questions.prompt: In Aristotle's scheme, what turns an aristocracy into an oligarchy?

options.label: The number of rulers doubles
options.rationale: Both are rule by a few; the difference is their aim.

options.label: A king takes over
options.rationale: That would be rule by one.

options.label: The few rule for their own good instead of the common good
The people start voting on every law

questions.explanation: Both are rule by a few. Aristocracy aims at the common good; oligarchy serves the rulers themselves, usually the wealthy.

questions.prompt: Kinds of Government checkpoint: which list puts these in order, oldest first?

options.label: Rome's republic → Venice's closing → Louis XIV → Sweden's 1974 text
Venice's closing → Rome's republic → Louis XIV → Sweden's 1974 text
options.rationale: The Roman Republic (509 BCE) is far older than 1297.

options.label: Rome's republic → Louis XIV → Venice's closing → Sweden's 1974 text
options.rationale: Venice's closing began in 1297, before Louis XIV (1643).

options.label: Louis XIV → Rome's republic → Sweden's 1974 text → Venice's closing
options.rationale: Rome's republic is the oldest by far.

questions.explanation: Roman Republic (509 BCE), Venice's Great Council begins closing (1297), Louis XIV's reign begins (1643), Sweden's Instrument of Government (1974).

questions.prompt: Kinds of Government checkpoint: which system gives regions powers protected by a constitution the center can't change alone?

options.label: A unitary state
options.rationale: In a unitary state, regional powers are delegated by the center.

options.label: A theocracy
options.rationale: Theocracy is about religious rule, not how power is split across the map.

options.label: An absolute monarchy
options.rationale: An absolute monarch holds unlimited central power.

options.label: A federal system

questions.explanation: Federal systems write the split of power into a constitution that can be changed only by extraordinary procedures.

questions.prompt: Kinds of Government checkpoint: Glarus voters raise their hands; Madison's republic elects a few. What's the difference?

options.label: Direct: citizens decide in person. Republic: elected representatives decide
Direct democracy has a monarch; a republic doesn't
options.rationale: Neither needs a monarch; the difference is who decides.

options.label: A republic lets citizens vote on every law in person
Only a republic holds votes of any kind
options.rationale: Glarus votes directly, by show of hands.

questions.explanation: In direct democracy citizens decide themselves; Madison's republic delegates government to a small number of citizens elected by the rest.
